items.title: Linear capillary free-surface model
items.design_state: Step 1 complete draft; readiness recorded separately.
items.statement:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, with absolute time $t\in I$ in seconds, and let $E$ be an oriented three-dimensional Euclidean affine space. The adopted Newtonian spacetime is the product $I\times E$. Define $\mathrm{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. A classical Cartesian inertial frame here is an adapted chart $\mathbf r:E\to\mathbb R^3$ that is an orientation-preserving affine isometry (its linear part lies in $\mathrm{SO}(3)$); its coordinates are measured in metres. Inertial charts are related by $t^*=t+t_0$ and $\mathbf r^*=Q\mathbf r+vt+a$, where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is constant, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is constant in metres per second, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is constant in metres. Thus “frame” means this adapted chart on Newtonian spacetime, not an observer congruence or a basis field. Write the selected chart coordinates as $(x_1,x_2,z)$, with horizontal coordinate $x=(x_1,x_2)$ and upward vertical coordinate $z$, all in metres, and let $e_z$ be the upward unit vector.

Fix $h>0$ metres and horizontal periods $L_1,L_2>0$ metres; set $\mathbb T^2_L:=\mathbb R^2/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z)$. For a scalar or vector field $f$ on $\mathbb T^2_L$, its lift is $\widetilde f(\widetilde x):=f([\widetilde x])$ on $\mathbb R^2$ and is periodic under each lattice translation $(L_1n_1,L_2n_2)$, $n_1,n_2\in\mathbb Z$. The notation $C^r$ for fields on $\mathbb T^2_L\times I$ or $\mathbb T^2_L\times[-h,0]\times I$ means that the lifted field has continuous ordinary coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$, with derivatives at $z=-h,0$ understood as continuous one-sided extensions. Horizontal coordinate partial derivatives are the corresponding derivatives of the periodic lift, so they are independent of the representative of a torus point. The flat reference liquid region is $\Omega_0:=\mathbb T^2_L\times(-h,0)$; the bottom $z=-h$ is a fixed solid bed and the real first-order surface-displacement coefficient is $\eta:\mathbb T^2_L\times I\to\mathbb R$, in metres. It is a formal perturbation coefficient, with no amplitude restriction such as $\eta>-h$. For an optional finite-displacement geometric interpretation on a compact time interval $K\subset I$, introduce a dimensionless $\varepsilon>0$ and the graph $z=\varepsilon\eta(x,t)$. Continuity on the compact horizontal cell times $K$ bounds $|\eta|$ by some finite $M$, so choosing $\varepsilon M<h$ keeps that graph above the bed. This geometric scaling imposes no bound on the formal coefficient and asserts no nonlinear solution or approximation accuracy. Horizontal periodic faces are mathematical identifications, not physical walls.

Adopt a homogeneous single-component liquid with constant mass density $\rho>0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, constant downward gravitational acceleration $-g e_z$ with $g>0$ in metres per second squared, and constant surface-tension coefficient $\gamma>0$ in newtons per metre, equivalently kilograms per second squared. Here $\rho$, $g$, $\gamma$, and the constant gas pressure $p_a$ are primitive inputs of this formulation; $h,L_1,L_2$ are fixed geometric parameters. For the optional finite-displacement geometry on $K$, define $\mathcal Q_{\ell,\varepsilon}:=\{(x,z,t):x\in\mathbb T^2_L,\ t\in K,\ -h<z<\varepsilon\eta(x,t)\}$. If an auxiliary liquid-pressure field $p_{\ell,\varepsilon}:\mathcal Q_{\ell,\varepsilon}\to\mathbb R$ in pascals is supplied, its liquid-side interface trace, when it exists, is $p_{\ell,\varepsilon}^\Gamma(x,t):=\lim_{z\uparrow\varepsilon\eta(x,t)}p_{\ell,\varepsilon}(x,z,t)$. No extension or smoothness of this pressure across the interface is assumed. The gas is modeled only by the prescribed constant pressure $p_a$; no gas momentum equation is included. This optional geometric pressure is distinct from the formal first-order pressure coefficient used below. The reduced first-order model does not construct such a nonlinear pressure family and has no independent pressure evolution equation. Its independent fields are the unrestricted formal displacement coefficient $\eta$ in metres and the scalar velocity-potential coefficient $\phi$ in metres squared per second, both on the fixed reference geometry. Define the full Cartesian gradient by $\nabla\phi:=(\partial_{x_1}\phi,\partial_{x_2}\phi,\partial_z\phi)$ and the derived fluid-velocity vector field by $u:=\nabla\phi:\mathbb T^2_L\times[-h,0]\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, in metres per second; there is no additive uniform velocity component. With $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$, define $\operatorname{div}u:=\partial_{x_1}u_1+\partial_{x_2}u_2+\partial_z u_3$ and $\operatorname{curl}u:=(\partial_{x_2}u_3-\partial_z u_2,\partial_z u_1-\partial_{x_1}u_3,\partial_{x_1}u_2-\partial_{x_2}u_1)$ using these Cartesian derivatives on the lifts. The model is inviscid, meaning no viscous-stress or viscous-dissipation terms are included; it is incompressible and irrotational, meaning $\operatorname{div}u=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}u=0$. On the torus this potential assumption is stronger than irrotationality alone, since a curl-free field need not be the gradient of a periodic scalar. Assume $\phi$ is at least $C^3$ and $\eta$ is at least $C^2$ in the periodic-lift sense just defined; derivatives below are classical.

Set $\nabla_h:=(\partial_{x_1},\partial_{x_2})$ and $\Delta_h:=\partial_{x_1}^2+\partial_{x_2}^2$ on the periodic lifts. For a horizontal vector field $v=(v_1,v_2)$, define $\nabla_h\cdot v:=\partial_{x_1}v_1+\partial_{x_2}v_2$ and $|v|^2:=v_1^2+v_2^2$. For the optional graph $z=\varepsilon\eta(x,t)$, the outward normal from liquid to gas is $n_\varepsilon:=(-\varepsilon\nabla_h\eta,1)/\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2|\nabla_h\eta|^2}$ and the signed curvature is $\kappa_\varepsilon:=-\nabla_h\cdot(\varepsilon\nabla_h\eta/\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2|\nabla_h\eta|^2})$, in inverse metres. The geometric liquid-minus-gas pressure law, whenever this optional pressure and trace are supplied, is $p_{\ell,\varepsilon}^\Gamma-p_a=\gamma\kappa_\varepsilon$. Its formal first-order curvature coefficient is $-\Delta_h\eta$. On the fixed reference slab define the first-order pressure coefficient $p^{(1)}:=-\rho\phi_t$, in pascals, in the potential gauge encoded by the dynamic equation below. The first-order interface pressure balance at the reference plane is $p^{(1)}(x,0,t)-\rho g\eta=-\gamma\Delta_h\eta$: the term $-\rho g\eta$ is the hydrostatic reference pressure evaluated to first order at height $\varepsilon\eta$. Substituting $p^{(1)}(x,0,t)=-\rho\phi_t(x,0,t)$ gives exactly the displayed linear dynamic condition. All coefficients are evaluated at $z=0$; neither $\phi$ nor its velocity is evaluated at $z=\varepsilon\eta$ or outside the fixed slab. At the fixed bed impose only impermeability, meaning zero normal fluid velocity, $u_z=0$, equivalently $\phi_z=0$ at $z=-h$. Since the bed is fixed, no-slip would additionally impose $u=0$ there; that condition is not imposed in this inviscid branch. The first-order kinematic equation below encodes surface motion at the reference plane; it is not a solid-wall condition or a claim of nonlinear material motion for the optional graph.

The selected first-order model is defined by retaining only terms linear in perturbations about the hydrostatic rest state $\eta=0$, $u=0$, and reference pressure $p_a-\rho g z$, then evaluating surface derivatives at $z=0$. Products of perturbations are discarded, with no error estimate for replacing a finite-amplitude flow by this linear model. On $\Omega_0\times I$ the adopted equations and boundary conditions are

$$\Delta_h\phi+\partial_z^2\phi=0,\qquad -h<z<0,$$

$$\partial_z\phi(x,-h,t)=0,$$

$$\partial_t\eta(x,t)=\partial_z\phi(x,0,t),\qquad \partial_t\phi(x,0,t)+g\eta(x,t)-\frac{\gamma}{\rho}\Delta_h\eta(x,t)=0.$$

These are model assumptions for the stated idealized regime. They assert no existence or uniqueness for the nonlinear free-boundary equations, no finite-amplitude approximation bound, and no empirical claim that a particular liquid satisfies this model.

items.physical_scope: Adopted first-order inviscid, homogeneous, incompressible and irrotational capillary-gravity waves in a periodic horizontal cell above a fixed impermeable bed, with constant density and surface tension and negligible air inertia. No viscosity, background current, finite-amplitude accuracy, solvability, or universal empirical validity is asserted.

items.title: Linear capillary-gravity wave dispersion
items.design_state: Step 1 complete draft; readiness recorded separately.
items.statement:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and let $E$ be an oriented three-dimensional Euclidean affine space, so the adopted Newtonian spacetime is $I\times E$ with absolute time $t\in I$. Define $\mathrm{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. Use an adapted Cartesian inertial chart $\mathbf r:E\to\mathbb R^3$, an orientation-preserving affine isometry whose linear part lies in $\mathrm{SO}(3)$; inertial charts are related by $t^*=t+t_0$ and $\mathbf r^*=Q\mathbf r+vt+a$, with constant $t_0$ in seconds, constant $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ constant in metres per second, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ constant in metres. In these coordinates, time is measured in seconds and spatial coordinates $(x_1,x_2,z)$ in metres. Fix $h>0$ metres and horizontal periods $L_1,L_2>0$ metres, and set $\mathbb T^2_L:=\mathbb R^2/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z)$. Use the real constant $\pi$ defined as twice the least positive zero of cosine. A field on $\mathbb T^2_L$ is interpreted by its lift $\widetilde f(\widetilde x)=f([\widetilde x])$ to $\mathbb R^2$, periodic under translations $(L_1n_1,L_2n_2)$ for integers $n_1,n_2$; on products with $I$ and $[-h,0]$, $C^r$ means the lifted field has continuous ordinary coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$, with continuous one-sided extensions at $z=-h,0$. Define $\nabla_h:=(\partial_{x_1},\partial_{x_2})$ and $\Delta_h:=\partial_{x_1}^2+\partial_{x_2}^2$ on these lifts. The real first-order fields are unrestricted formal perturbation coefficients, rather than finite-displacement interfaces: $\phi:\mathbb T^2_L\times[-h,0]\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $\eta:\mathbb T^2_L\times I\to\mathbb R$ are those of the postulated model; they are at least $C^3$ and $C^2$ respectively, with units metres squared per second and metres. The model parameters are constant density $\rho>0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, downward gravitational acceleration $-g e_z$ with $g>0$ in metres per second squared, and surface tension $\gamma>0$ in newtons per metre. They satisfy

$$\Delta_h\phi+\partial_z^2\phi=0\quad(-h<z<0),\qquad \partial_z\phi(x,-h,t)=0,$$

$$\partial_t\eta(x,t)=\partial_z\phi(x,0,t),\qquad \partial_t\phi(x,0,t)+g\eta(x,t)-\frac{\gamma}{\rho}\Delta_h\eta(x,t)=0.$$

Let $\mathbb C:=\mathbb R[X]/(X^2+1)$ be the complex field and $i:=[X]$, so $i^2=-1$. Let $\exp:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ be the series-defined complex exponential, $\exp w:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}w^n/n!$. For $m=(m_1,m_2)\in\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}$ define the wavevector $\mathbf k:=2\pi(m_1/L_1,m_2/L_2)\in\mathbb R^2$ in inverse metres and its magnitude $k:=|\mathbf k|>0$. The phase terms $\mathbf k\cdot\widetilde x$ and $\omega t$ are dimensionless. For $\omega\in\mathbb C$ in inverse seconds, define the mode factor on the quotient torus by

$$q_m([x],t):=\exp\bigl(i(\mathbf k\cdot\widetilde x-\omega t)\bigr),$$

where $\widetilde x\in\mathbb R^2$ is any representative of $[x]\in\mathbb T^2_L$. If $\widetilde x$ changes by $(L_1n_1,L_2n_2)$, the phase in parentheses changes by $2\pi N$ for $N=m_1n_1+m_2n_2\in\mathbb Z$; the complex-exponential addition law and $e^{i\pi}=-1$ give $\exp(2\pi iN)=1$ for every integer $N$ (by repeated addition for $N\ge0$ and $\exp(w)\exp(-w)=1$ for $N<0$), so $q_m$ is independent of the representative. Its lift is smooth, and $\Delta_hq_m=-k^2q_m$.

A complex mode of angular frequency $\omega$ is a pair $\eta_c(x,t)=Hq_m(x,t)$ and $\phi_c(x,z,t)=F(z)q_m(x,t)$ satisfying the complex-linear extension of the displayed model equations, with $H\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ in metres and $F\in C^2([-h,0],\mathbb C)$ in metres squared per second; here $C^2([-h,0],\mathbb C)$ means that the first two ordinary derivatives exist on $(-h,0)$ and extend continuously to both endpoints. The real and imaginary parts of any such mode are real-valued formal coefficient solutions of the real linear model, with no restriction on $|H|$. Optional finite-displacement graphs are $z=\varepsilon\eta$ with sufficiently small dimensionless $\varepsilon$ on compact time windows as in the postulate; they impose no amplitude bound on these coefficients and no nonlinear-solution claim. For real $s$ write $e^s:=\exp(s)$, $\sinh s:=(e^s-e^{-s})/2$, $\cosh s:=(e^s+e^{-s})/2$, and $\tanh s:=\sinh s/\cosh s$. Such a nonzero mode exists exactly when

$$\omega^2=\left(gk+\frac{\gamma}{\rho}k^3\right)\tanh(kh),$$

For these hypotheses the right-hand side is positive because $k,h,g,\gamma,\rho>0$ and $\tanh(kh)>0$. Thus for each $m$ the two frequencies $\omega=\pm\sqrt{(gk+(\gamma/\rho)k^3)\tanh(kh)}$, with the positive real square root, admit a nonzero mode. This is a conditional prediction of the stated first-order model, not a measurement or a claim that any actual fluid realizes every assumption.

items.title: Positive gravity and capillary modal restoring terms
items.design_state: Step 1 complete draft; readiness recorded separately.
items.statement:
Use $\mathbb C:=\mathbb R[X]/(X^2+1)$ with $i:=[X]$, the series-defined complex exponential $\exp w:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}w^n/n!$, and $\pi$ defined as twice the least positive zero of cosine.

Fix periods $L_1,L_2>0$ metres and let $\mathbb T^2_L:=\mathbb R^2/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z)$. Define horizontal derivatives by differentiating the $L$-periodic lift to $\mathbb R^2$, and set $\Delta_h:=\partial_{x_1}^2+\partial_{x_2}^2$. Fix an integer lattice mode $m=(m_1,m_2)\in\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}$ and define its wavevector and magnitude by $\mathbf k:=2\pi(m_1/L_1,m_2/L_2)$ in inverse metres and $k:=|\mathbf k|>0$. For any representative $\widetilde x\in\mathbb R^2$ of $[x]\in\mathbb T^2_L$, define the horizontal mode factor $q_m^h([x]):=\exp(i\mathbf k\cdot\widetilde x)$. A change of representative by $(L_1n_1,L_2n_2)$ changes its exponent by $2\pi iN$, where $N=m_1n_1+m_2n_2\in\mathbb Z$; the exponential addition law and $\exp(i\pi)=-1$ give $\exp(2\pi iN)=1$ for every integer $N$ (by repeated addition for $N\ge0$ and $\exp(w)\exp(-w)=1$ for $N<0$), so $q_m^h$ is well-defined. The identity $\exp(i\mathbf k\cdot\widetilde x)\exp(-i\mathbf k\cdot\widetilde x)=\exp(0)=1$ also shows $q_m^h$ never vanishes. Its periodic lift has $\Delta_hq_m^h=-k^2q_m^h$. Thus, for any unrestricted nonzero formal coefficient amplitude $H\in\mathbb C$ in metres, the nonzero horizontal mode $\eta_m:=Hq_m^h$ satisfies $\Delta_h\eta_m=-k^2\eta_m$. For real $s$, write $e^s:=\exp(s)$ and define $\sinh s:=(e^s-e^{-s})/2$, $\cosh s:=(e^s+e^{-s})/2$, and $\tanh s:=\sinh s/\cosh s$. In the adopted finite-depth linear model with $h>0$ metres, $\rho>0$ kilograms per cubic metre, $g>0$ metres per second squared and $\gamma>0$ newtons per metre, its capillary contribution to the restoring coefficient is $\gamma k^2/\rho>0$ and adds to the positive gravity coefficient $g$. The model angular frequency $\omega$ in inverse seconds therefore satisfies $\omega^2=(gk+(\gamma/\rho)k^3)\tanh(kh)>0$. No finite-displacement constraint is imposed on this formal coefficient: optional geometric displacements are scaled by a sufficiently small dimensionless factor on compact time windows as in the postulate. This is a symbolic conditional model example; it reports no observation or numerical measurement.
